courses.title: Jazz Appreciation: Jazz, American Culture, and Global Contexts
courses.description: This course introduces students to jazz music and its connections to both African-American culture and global social-historical contexts. The first half of the semester focuses on the development of jazz in the United States, surveying the rise of the music as an African-American art form over the course of the twentieth century, with attention to blues, ragtime, swing, bebop, modal jazz, free jazz, and fusion. The second half of the semester considers jazz as a transnationally circulating cultural form that is both a product of and a contributor to globalizing trends, examining jazz’s circulations and permutations in contexts ranging from 1930s Shanghai to present-day West Africa. Through this course, students will gain a familiarity with the history of jazz, some of its major innovators, and its musical characteristics. Critical and close listening will be an important aspect of this course; through in-depth audition and discussion of musical examples, students will gain aural skills that increase their appreciation and understanding of jazz music. At the same time, by examining jazz in relation to issues including race, ethnicity, political consciousness, globalization, and economics, students will develop skills in thinking critically about music’s connections to social, cultural, and historical contexts. No musical background or previous study of music is required.

* Be able to identify, comprehend, and describe important musical characteristics of different styles of jazz, and develop close listening skills that increase their appreciation and understanding of the music
* Cultivate skills in thinking critically about music’s connections to social, cultural, and historical contexts and issues
* Acquire global perspectives on music making, and learn to situate their musical perspectives and experiences within a global context

courses.title: Understanding Musicals: Broadway and Beyond
courses.description:
How does the music work in Broadway shows? How does music interact with the plot and drama? How are megamusicals like Phantom of the Opera and Les Misérables different from the other musicals? What can we listen for to enhance our appreciation for musicals? This course explores different perspectives of studying and appreciating the musical arts of the modern musical theatre, covering areas such as analyses of the musical elements, storytelling through motifs and themes, aesthetics and criticism, as well as gender issues, politics, and other realms of contextual studies. Examples will be drawn from the Broadway musicals since the 1950s, musical films, as well as examples from the western classical tradition if deemed necessary.

Active, analytical, and critical listening will be integral to understanding the materials and concepts in this class. Students are expected and encouraged to practice active listening and analysis beyond the classroom setting. No previous experience is required. This course is not for music majors.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for Music Majors. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of the course, students are expected to:

* Describe musical events and progression in melody, harmony, texture, orchestration, and music-text relationship and critically evaluate a piece through different parameters.
* Analyze the musical languages and devices used music theatre.
* Develop skills to listen analytically to a large-scale staged music production.
* Contextualize the musicals in their political, social, and cultural environment.
* Understand the creation of unity and coherence in a piece of musical work.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Theory of Integration and Difference
Proposed by McMillin, the theory of integration and differences discusses two layers of time in a musical, namely the time of the plot progression and the time of the song and dance. Different musicals have markedly different approaches in dealing with the two layers of time, which affects their overall effectiveness storytelling.
2. Narration and Technology
This lecture discusses how development in stage technology has changed the mode of narration in musicals, and how technology is integrated with music.
3. Understanding Leitmotifs in Musicals
This lecture discusses how musical ideas symbolize different ideas and characters in a musical theatre work, and how those ideas are transformed to assist with storytelling.
4. Social Issues in Musicals
This lecture discusses how musicals interact with the society through the lenses of politics, religion, gender issues, and other phenomena, exploring the reflection of societal values as well as the art works’ attempt to change established ideas.
5. Cultural Perspectives on Musicals
This lecture explores the portrayal of different cultures through the musical theatre, and how they affect aspects of musical creation, staging, and casting in the work.
6. The Phenomenon of Megamusicals
This lecture explores the defining characteristics of megamusicals in the 80s such as Phantom of the Opera, Les Misérables, and Cats, from the gradual adaption of the “sung-through” style to the new marketing components such as TV commercials, merchandise, souvenirs, etc.
7. Musical Innovations in Music Theatre
The lecture discusses the use of innovative musical devices in musical theatre, such as pointillism in lyrics and music, minimalism, polytonality, as well as the fusion of styles such as hip-hop and metal rock in musicals.
8. Recent Development in Musicals
This lecture discusses recent developments in musicals with a focus on musicals from the 21st century, such as La La Land, Hamilton, and other local examples.

courses.description: This course aims to provide an opportunity for students to understand the intellectual history of China from the late Qing dynasty to contemporary China. It will discuss the impact of Western ideologies on Chinese culture, as well as evaluate how they influenced Chinese intellectuals and modern Chinese society. This course integrates SDGs by discussing how western education influenced modern China. (SDG#4 Quality Education) How the contemporary Chinese intellectual tried to eliminate inequality and poverty by introducing education and new ideologies from the West. (SDG#1 No Poverty) Poverty, the developments of quality education and women rights in modern China will be examined. (SDG#10 Reduced Inequality SDG#16 Peace and Justice Strong Institutions) Students are able to exam several modern China SDGs developments through historical aspects, including SDG#1 No Poverty SDG#4 Quality Education SDG#10 Reduced Inequality SDG#16 Peace and Justice Strong Institutions.

courses.subject: UGED
courses.title: Study of Christianity
courses.description:
(UGED1520 is double-coded with CURE1124.)

The primary aim of this course is to provide students a broad and comprehensive understanding of the Christian faith through introducing its characteristics, traditions, history, scripture, theology and ethics. It helps students to analyse critically the various forms of Christianity and appreciate the richness of the Christian religion that exerts so great influences on human civilizations. Through interdisciplinary dialogues, this course also aims at helping students to see how the Christian faith understands and deals with problems, predicaments, political and ethical dilemmas of humanity.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGED1520 is double-coded with CURE1124. 
Not for Cultural Studies; Public Humanities; Religious Studies; Theology Majors; and students who have taken CURE1124. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge:

* To achieve proper understanding of Christianity as a global phenomenon and some of the representative manifestations of Christianity in various local contexts.
* To obtain a comprehensive knowledge of the major aspects of Christian faith, especially its views of the meaning of human life.
* To have a basic understanding of the methodology involved in the multidisciplinary study of Christianity.

Skills:

* To be able to use the analytical framework and hermeneutical tools for the academic studies of the religious phenomena related to Christianity.
* To be capable of relating what have been leant from this course to some other academic disciplines.
* To have the ability to reflect critically on one’s own cultural and / or religious tradition.

Attitudes:

* To treasure the value of human life and be sensitive to the related ethical responsibilities.
* To appreciate the diversity within particular cultural and / religious tradition.
* To become more respectful to others’ religions, worldviews and values.

1. To appreciate the artistry of key Taiwan writers and their works.

2. To master the methodology of analyzing Taiwan Literature.

4. To be better prepared for immersing themselves in Taiwan Literature.

1. 臺灣文學的發展概況

從臺灣歷史說起：臺灣原住民、荷蘭殖民時期、鄭成功在臺灣

2. 臺灣文學中不同文類的藝術特色

現代主義小說、圖象詩、現代散文等

3. 臺灣文學的重要作家及作品

小說：白先勇〈冬夜〉、陳映真〈將軍族〉、黃春明〈兒子的大玩偶〉、朱天文〈世紀末的華麗〉

王德威從文學角度看歷史、史書美的華語語系研究、陳芳明的臺灣新文學史

《他們在島嶼寫作‧逍遙遊》

1. The development of Taiwan Literature

courses.description: This course examines the role of music and sound in film. It enables students with no training in music or media studies to better appreciate the art of film music.Through lectures and assignments that comprise viewing, listening, and reading, students explore the work of many composers and directors and gain skills to critically evaluate what they see and hear.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for Music Majors.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
Through this course, students will have:

* Expanded their knowledge of film and music, and acquired a broad appreciation of the methods of film composers
* Developed an understanding of how music and other sounds interact with visual images to communicate ideas
* Enhanced their critical skills and developed the habit of questioning the meaning of what they see and hear
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Introduction
Overview of the course, objectives, introduction to the study of film music. Recommended readings cover elements of film and music.
2. The language of film music
Terminology – purely musical elements: dissonance, major-minor, style topics, timbre, atonality, music in the film context: diegetic & non-diegetic, acoustics, audio dissolve; synchronization, counterpoint, clarity and false clarity, presence of absence, structural use of music, the montage and performance scenes.
3. Post-WWII science fiction and the sound of technology
The place of timbre in sci-fi films of the 1940s and ‘50s, focusing on the introduction of electronic sound in films such as *The Day the Earth Stood Still* and *Forbidden Planet*
4. Vangelis and the sound of technology in the 1980s
Composer Vangelis’s use of synthesizers in films of the 1980s and ‘90s, including action films (*Missing*), historical drama (*Chariots of Fire*), and the classic genre-blending sci-fi, *Blade Runner*.
5. Rachel Portman and the sound of tradition
Scores from the English film composer Rachael Portman, best known for her work on literary and historical dramas, such as *Chocolat*, *Cider House Rules*, *Emma*, *Never Let Me Go*, and *One Day*
6. Bernard Herrmann: master film composer
Broad overview of one of the most successful film composers of the post-WWII era. Examples include excerpts from *Citizen Kane*, *The Ghost and Mrs. Muir*, several of his scores for Alfred Hitchcock (*Vertigo*, *Psycho*, *North By Northwest*), and his final score, for Martin Scorsese’s *Taxi Driver* (1976)
7. Ennio Morricone: spaghetti westerns and more
One of the most original film composers: Ennio Morricone. Examples drawn from his classic 1960s spaghetti westerns of Sergio Leone (*Once Upon a Time in the West*), to big-budget Hollywood (*The Mission*, *The Legend of 1900*) and European films (*Malèna*, *Cinema Paradiso*)
8. Zhao Jiping (and Zhang Yimou)
Politics and culture: classic Chinese films of the 1980s and ‘90s, including *Red Sorghum* and *Raise the Red Lantern*
9. Stanley Kubrick and classical music
A filmmaker known for his borrowing from classical music for the soundtracks of his films. Examples from historical dramas (*Barry Lyndon*), war films (Full Metal Jacket), classic horror (*The Shining*), science fiction (*2001, A Space Odyssey*), and his final film (*Eyes Wide Shut*)
10. The pop compilation soundtrack
For several decades popular music has provided the readymade soundtracks – from such classics of the 1960s as *The Graduate* and *Easy Rider* to the more obscure uses of pop music in the films of Quentin Tarantino (*Pulp Fiction*, *Kill Bill*).
11. Ang Lee and the period drama
Wide-ranging work of Taiwanese-US director, focusing on the use of music in period dramas: *The Ice Storm* (1997), *Brokeback Mountain* (2005), and *Lust, Caution* (2007)
12. Comedy: the sound of humour and Course overview
The course ends with a lecture on music in comedy films – from early animation and the films of Charlie Chaplin to the works of and Stephen Chow (周星馳).

courses.title: Global Popular Music: Listening Across Cultures
courses.description: This course introduces students to global genres of popular music as they are created and understood in diverse local contexts. We take a global perspective on the development of popular music beginning in the early twentieth century, examining the rise of interconnected entertainment industries from New York to Shanghai and Cairo. We extend our perspectives on popular music in contemporary cultural contexts through case studies including hip-hop, heavy metal, reggae, highlife, and other styles. Along the way, we consider how popular music reflects and shapes cultural identities; serves as a vehicle for nationalism, community building, or protest; and articulates perspectives on globality. The course therefore serves as an introduction to the cultural study of music, drawing on diverse disciplinary perspectives and critical methodologies from ethnomusicology, sociology, cultural studies, and media studies. Classes are structured around interactive lectures, in-depth collective listening activities, small group discussions, and in-class assignments. No background in music is expected or required, but a love of popular music is welcome.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for Music Majors.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
* Gain familiarity with diverse genres of popular music and how they relate to local contexts and global cultures
* Be able to identify, comprehend, and describe important musical characteristics of different genres of popular music, and develop close listening skills that increase their appreciation and understanding of the music
* Cultivate skills in thinking critically about music’s connections to social, cultural, and historical contexts and issues, and develop understanding of diverse interdisciplinary approaches to the cultural study of music and its relationship to issues including politics, race, ethnicity, gender, nationalism, and globalization
* Acquire global perspectives on popular music, and learn to situate their musical perspectives and experiences within broader historical and transnational contexts
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Part I – The Emergence of Global Popular Music**

This unit introduces the historical foundations of contemporary popular music and the development of global music industries beginning in the early twentieth century. Through case studies from North America, East Asia, and the Middle East, students examine how new technologies, colonial histories, and transnational cultural exchange shaped the emergence of popular music traditions in different parts of the world.

1. Introducing Popular Music

2. Minstrel Shows, Tin Pan Alley, and North American Contexts

3. Shidaiqu in Republican Era Shanghai and the Birth of Popular Music Industries in East Asia

4. Umm Kulthum, Tarab, and the Golden Age of Arabic Popular Music

* *Part II – Black Atlantic Popular Musics**

In this unit, students examine the global influence of Black popular music traditions through case studies from the Caribbean, West Africa, and the United States. Focusing on reggae, Afrobeat, and hip-hop, students explore how music reflects and shapes cultural identities, and how Black cultural heritage has shaped the development and global circulation of contemporary popular music.

5. Reggae, Dub, and Rastafari in Jamaican Society

6. Highlife, Afrobeat, and West African Popular Music

7. Hip-Hop, Part 1: Hip-Hop Culture’s Birth in New York City

8. Hip-Hop, Part 2: Hip-Hop in Global Contexts

* *Part III – Global Genres in Local Contexts**

This unit explores how globally circulating musical genres are reinterpreted in diverse cultural settings, and how artists and audiences use popular music to express feelings, localized perspectives, and social concerns within an increasingly interconnected world.

9. Rock Music, Politics, and Protest in the Global 1960s

10. Heavy Metal in the Global South

11. Japanese Enka: Popular Music, Emotion, and Affect

12. Popular Music and Globality: Indie Music in Indonesia

courses.title: Existentialism and Literature
courses.description:
(UGED2172 is double-coded with ENGE2220.)
This course looks at the close relationship between existentialist philosophy and literature. Existentialism is a philosophical movement that focuses on human existence and the challenges of choice, freedom, and responsibility in the modern world. We will explore a variety of existentialist positions—including those of Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Sartre, and de Beauvoir—to understand how existentialist thought constitutes an important intellectual context for many themes in modern literature, including authenticity, alienation, and anxiety. Authors to be discussed include Kafka, Dostoevsky, Ionesco, Camus, Beckett and others. Students interested in literary representations of the existential challenges of the human condition are welcome to attend this course.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGED2172 is double-coded with ENGE2220. 
Not for English; English Studies and English Language Education (ELED) Majors; and students who have taken ENGE2220. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of the course, students should be able to:

* analyze and synthesize some of the most distinct themes and concepts in the existentialist movement
* analyze and evaluate various approaches to reading existentialist themes in modern literature
* appreciate the importance, relevance, and value of existentialist themes in modern literature
* produce a well-reasoned critical essay
courses.course_syllabus:
* **Week 1**
+ Topic: Introduction (syllabus, reading material exam issues)
- Description: In this lecture, we will go through all the practical issues related to this course.

* **Week 2**
+ Topic: Introduction to Existentialism and Literature
- Description: This lecture provides a broad overview of the historical and intellectual background of existentalist literature, and some of the major ideas associated with this movement.

* **Week 3**
+ Topic: Choice and Responsibility
- Description: In Week 3, we will explore how Sartre’s notion of ‘choice’ plays a crucial role in modern literature, including *Nausea* and “Drive my Car.”

* **Week 4**
+ Topic: Freedom and Anxiety
- Description: This lecture explores the difference between ‘fear’ and ‘anxiety’, and how this difference is often thematized in modern literature and art.

* **Week 5**
+ Topic: The Ethics of Existence
- Description: This week, we explore the relationship between individual freedom and moral responsibility.

* **Week 6**
+ Topic: Alienation and Guilt
- Description: Guilt and alienation are some of the major themes in existentialist literature. This lecture explains how Kafka and Ionesco address these themes.

* **Week 7**
+ Topic: Authentic Living, Das Man, Subjects and Objects
- Description: What is meant by an ‘authentic’ life—as opposed to a life of gestures, illusions, and performances? We will explore this question through a discussion of Heidegger’s philosophy and the film *The Truman Show.*

* **Week 8**
+ Topic: The Absurd and the Meaning of Life
- Description: One of the best known existentalist writers, Albert Camus introduced the philosophy of the absurd. This lecture provides an introduction to this philosophy through a discussion of the novel *The Stranger.*

* **Week 9**
+ Topic: Repetition and the Eternal Recurrence of the Same
- Description: Nietzsche formulates a way of thinking about the repetitiveness of existence, and this lecture will apply these thoughts in connection with a discussion of the film *Groundhog Day.*

* **Week 10**
+ Topic: Language and Presence
- Description: This lecture focuses on the role of language in existentialist literature, and more specifically the gap between language and reality.
* **Week 11**
+ Topic: Waiting, Inaction, Boredom
- Description: Accompanying the sense of individual freedom, protagonists in existentialist literature often experience a sense of purposelessness. The lecture will discuss this challenge in connection with works by Beckett and Coppola.
* **Week 12**
+ Topic: Memory, Regret, and Existence
- Description: The course began with Sartre’s notion of choice; this penultimate lecture looks at the time when these choices have been made, and when people will have to live with these decisions.
* **Week 13**
+ Course Summary & Conclusion

courses.subject: UGED
courses.title: Understanding Chinese Art through Exhibitions
courses.description:
(UGED2286 is double-coded with CURE2406.)

The exhibition has become a site of knowledge production and a prominent and diverse part of contemporary culture. Regarding “Chinese art” as a social constructed concept, the course uses “exhibition” as an entry point to engage with issues concerning Chinese art and to explore the role played by exhibitions in the formation of the knowledge of Chinese art. It introduces the current theories and debates on the theory and history of exhibition, and the display methods, examining the changing concept of Chinese art and curatorial practices through detailed analysis of case studies. The first part of the course traces the formation of the concept of “Chinese art” by looking closely at the history of exhibitions on Chinese objects from the late Qing dynasty to the early twentieth century. The second part examines important exhibitions that have shaped our understanding of Chinese art. Structured thematically, the course discusses the curatorial concepts of selective significant international exhibitions on Chinese art, and investigate how scholarly research has been transformed into exhibitions which have shaped our understanding of Chinese art, constructed identity and been deployed for political ends.

Upon the completion of the course, students will be able to:

Each day, our life is flooded with thoughts and emotions aroused by noises outside and inside of us. Do these thoughts and emotions support the real purpose of our life, bringing fulfillment and happiness? Or do they make our life an endless cycle of stress, anger, fear, and even hopelessness? The course offers an orientation into mindfulness meditation as a possible way of “resetting,” at personal and inter-personal levels. Emphasis is on reflective participation, supplemented by knowledge of basic concepts and principles.

From the formal practice of sitting cross-legged and quietly counting the breaths to the informal practice of embracing each moment in daily life, students will be guided to cultivate samma sati, or “right mindfulness,” one of the Eightfold Paths to end suffering. Mindfulness meditation (MM) is grounded in ancient Buddhist sutras named Anapanasati (“mindfulness breathing”) and Satipatthana (“foundation of mindfulness”) and 2,500 years of lay and monastic practice. It aims for the practitioner to develop one-pointed concentration on the body, feelings, mind, and dharmas (phenomena), and thereby to reflect on their impermanence, comprehend no-self, and cultivate loving kindness. Over the past decades, a whole range of secular mindfulness practices, or mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs), have emerged to serve therapeutic and educational purposes. Students may also explore one or more of such modern applications, and ponder the contribution of mindfulness training to good health and well-being (Sustainable Development Goal 3), and to Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) as a whole.

The course will take students on a one-week retreat in a Buddhist meditation centre, preceded by readings and presentations on relevant topics, and followed by a personal reflection and a mini-research on the experience. Through undisturbed practice of mindfulness meditation away from home and along with peers and monastics, students will master the basic skills of the formal practice and begin to develop a habit of mindful living. Hopefully, they will cultivate a sense of self-compassion and connectedness with fellow human beings that fosters emotion management, harmonious relation and wise social action.

courses.course_syllabus:
The **major concepts and practices** to be covered include, but are not limited to, the following aspects of mindfulness meditation:

* *(1) Basic Concepts and Principles**

* Non-duality in the *Heart Sutra*/*Heart of Understanding*
* The Buddha’s story: *dukkha* (suffering), *metta* (loving kindness), *samadhi* (meditation)
* Four Noble Truths: from *dukkha* to impermanence, no-self, dependent origination
* Eightfold Path: *sila* (morality), *samadhi* (meditation), *prajna* (insight)
* The Four Immeasurables: from *metta* to *karuna*, *mudita*, and *upekkha*
* Right *Samadhi* 正定: stages of *dhyana* (meditation 禪定), *ekaggata* (one-pointedness/心一境性), *vipassana* (insight-meditation 內觀)
* Right Mindfulness 正念: *Sati* (bare awareness): (impermanence of) five aggregates, four foundations of mindfulness, seven factors of awakening, five remembrances

* *(2) Mindfulness Meditation**

* Body as temple: awareness of body (breaths, bodily sensations, sound), feelings, and thoughts; non-judgmental observation; letting go; habit energy
* Sitting Meditation: posture, focus on breaths and sound
* Others methods of meditation (e.g., walking, eating, tea sharing, flower arrangement, drum, forest bathing, etc.)
* Five Mindfulness Trainings

* *(3) Study of the Mind**

* Mind-only School: the eight levels of consciousness
* The neuroscientist’s perspective

* *(4) Developments in Modern Times**

* *Personal*: Dealing with anger, fear, etc.; Mindfulness-based Stress Reduction
* *Inter-personal*: Nonviolent Communication
* *Socio-political*: Engaged Buddhism
* *Nature:* Forest Bathing

* *(5) Mindfulness and Sustainability**

* Mindfulness for Health and Well-being (Sustainable Development Goal 3)
* Mindfulness as Education for Sustainable Development (ESD)

The course will be **implemented** in three steps:

1. Before the retreat, students must fulfill the following requirements to qualify for participation (and sponsorship, if any) for the retreat:

- Attendance at two lectures for a general introduction to Buddhist mindfulness and meditation practice (with references to the *Satipatthana Sutra* and the *Anapanasati Sutra*); with a quiz given at the end of the second lecture, and one or more workshops on different forms of meditation

- Report on a book/article on one of the following topics: (1) Engaged Buddhism, (2) Mindfulness Meditations, (3) Nonviolent Communication, (4) Emotion Management (dealing with anger, fear, etc.), (5) Mindfulness-based Interventions (e.g., MBRS, MBCT, etc.), and (6) Mindfulness and Neuroscience. A list of recommended books and articles will be offered for students’ choice; students may also propose their own titles and seek the instructor’s approval; and

- Participation in a seminar to share presentations on the book/article report (subject to arrangement at the retreat centre chosen, the presentation may take place during the retreat).
2. During the retreat, students will practice periods of silence, sitting meditation and other forms of guided meditation, and learn to be mindful throughout the day, in eating, walking, working, exercising, etc. They will be required to attend talks and ceremonies, and share their reflections and raise questions in gatherings during the retreat. Students must participate in all activities of the retreat with satisfactory performance to qualify for any sponsorship available for the trip.
3. After the retreat, students will write a final report to reflect on the experience and to conduct a mini-research on a topic of interest emerging from the retreat, the result of which they will present at a final student seminar.

courses.description:
(UGED2315 is double-coded with FAAS2113.)

The survey introduces the art and material culture of pre-20th century Asia with particular attention paid to trans-regional and cross-cultural interactions. Select artistic traditions in West (mainly, Iran), South (India, Sri Lanka, and the Himalayas), Southeast (Indonesia, Burma, Thai, Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam), and Inner (Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, and Mongolia) will be examined against their philosophical, religious, socio-political, economic, aesthetic, and technological backgrounds. Major themes include (1) the rise of civilizations, (2) developments of various artistic forms and media, (3) tombs and funerary paraphernalia, (4) the spread of Buddhism, Hinduism, Islamism, and other worldviews across the region, and (5) Indianization and Sinicization.

courses.title: Understanding Comic Arts
courses.description:
(UGED2326 is double-coded with CURE2051.)

Nowadays comic strip has become one of the major forms of visual narratives in our culture. Both comics and film are visual arts originally developed within the period of late 19th century and early 20th century. Although film has long ago established its artistic legitimacy, comic art still struggle for recognition. However, as Will Eisner put it, comic strip is a “Sequential Art” and has its own unique aesthetic nature. This course tries to inquire the governing aesthetic principles of comics and investigate its unique method of expression. We will also try to delineate the special communication mode of comics and its relationship with different aspects of modern society and culture. Students will learn to appreciate comic art from different perspectives, and strengthen analytical skills for visual media.

courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Through the lectures, students will recognize the aesthetic nature of sequential art and locate the humanistic values and meanings of comic arts for modern society and culture.

2. Through tutorial discussions, student will apply the analytical skills and formal methods to interpret comic and visual texts.

3. Through mid-term assignment (research portfolio on the visual representation of comics), student will distinguish, compare, analyze and criticize different visual and multimedia sources.

4. Through final paper, student will prepare and manage to do an academic research on visual representation.

5. Student will aware, judge and appraise the practical values of the analytical skills and historical knowledge provided by this course after they complete the mid-term assignment and final paper.

courses.description: "The Book of Changes" (Yijing) is a highly venerated and influential classic that has made far-reaching impacts on the Chinese religion, philosophy, politics and medicine. It has a far greater significance for the Chinese culture as a book of wisdom than a divination manual, by offering a wealth of knowledge and insights about the cosmos, nature, and life. It shows us the ways to cultivate virtue, enhance ability and perceive wisdom by living our lives and making judgments in harmony with the changing forces of the universe. The store of ancient wisdom accumulated in this classic is often still relevant to our contemporary world that is in constant and rapid technological, social and political changes. Through guided reading of the key notions and themes encapsulated in some selected hexagrams, students may draw from the wellspring of profound wisdom in the "The Book of Changes" to stimulate their reflection on the approach of life, the way of looking at the world, and the recurring issues facing humanity.

courses.title: Being Human in the Age of AI: An Introduction to Digital Ethics
courses.description:
(UGED2329 is double-coded with CURE2008.)
Artificial intelligence (AI) and data science are reshaping every aspect of contemporary life—from how we work and communicate to how decisions are made about health, education, and governance. This course introduces the ethical, social, and philosophical issues that arise from these technologies. Students will examine topics such as algorithmic bias, data surveillance, automation, misinformation, and AI’s impact on human agency and creativity. Drawing on philosophical frameworks, scientific research, and real-world case studies, the course encourages students to think critically about how technological systems embody values and power structures, and how they can be governed responsibly. The course aims to develop students’ ethical reasoning, cross-disciplinary understanding, and ability to articulate informed positions on emerging technologies. Through a team-based learning approach, students engage in weekly readings, discussions, and collaborative writing exercises that cultivate both independent judgment and cooperative problem-solving. No technical background is required.

courses.learning_outcomes:
* *Students should be able to:**

1. Analyze and Apply Ethical Frameworks: Identify and apply key ethical theories (e.g., virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism) to evaluate the design and deployment of AI and data-driven technologies.
2. Evaluate Global Societal Impacts: Critically assess the social and political implications of algorithmic systems—such as bias, surveillance, and data colonialism—integrating diverse global and cross-cultural perspectives.
3. Construct Ethical Arguments: Formulate and defend informed, persuasive positions on the responsible governance and ethical use of emerging technologies in contemporary society.
4. Collaborate and Communicate Effectively: Work productively in teams to synthesize complex ethical ideas and communicate them clearly through collaborative writing and oral presentations.
5. Practice Critical Reflexivity: Reflect on one’s own assumptions, values, and agency as a user, designer, or citizen within an AI-mediated world.
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Week 1: Introduction – Value and Technology**
How do technology and human values intersect? Explore Heidegger’s and Bryson’s perspectives on technology as a cultural practice, and discuss technology’s role in shaping human existence and meaning.

* *Week 2: Foundations of AI and Data Science**
What are artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data science? Examine foundational concepts, basic algorithms, and the societal narratives that frame technological innovation.

* *Week 3: Ethical Frameworks – Virtue, Duty, and Utility**
How can ethics guide technology? Introduce virtue ethics and human flourishing, Kantian deontology, and utilitarian reasoning as frameworks for evaluating technological decisions.

* *Week 4: Data and Surveillance Capitalism**
How does data become a source of power? Investigate the political economy of data extraction, corporate surveillance, and the ethics of privacy, consent, and digital autonomy.

* *Week 5: Algorithmic Bias and Fairness**
How do biases enter algorithms? Analyze social and technical dimensions of algorithmic bias, justice, accountability, and transparency through real-world case studies.

* *Week 6: AI as a Mirror of Humanity**
In what ways does AI reflect us? Explore how machine learning systems reproduce human cognition, prejudice, and creativity, and question the limits of “artificial” intelligence.

* *Week 7: Data Colonialism and Global Inequality**
How does AI reproduce global power asymmetries? Study postcolonial and Global South critiques of data extraction, digital labor, and the ethics of global governance.

* *Week 8: Responsibility and the “Moral Gap”**
Who is accountable for AI’s actions? Examine the “responsibility gap” in autonomous systems and discuss moral agency, liability, and ethical design.

* *Week 9: Online Manipulation and Persuasive Design**
How do digital platforms shape behavior? Investigate the behavioral economics of attention, nudging, dark patterns, and the ethics of algorithmic persuasion in social media.

* *Week 10: Deepfakes, Truth, and Misinformation**
What happens when truth becomes malleable? Discuss the epistemology of misinformation, authenticity in AI-generated media, and implications for democracy and public trust.

* *Week 11: Gamification and the Algorithmic Self**
How does gamification transform communication and learning? Analyze the role of AI in shaping motivation, reward systems, and social interaction in digital environments.

* *Week 12: In-Class Essay Examination**
Students compose a critical essay applying one or more ethical frameworks to a contemporary issue in AI and data ethics. Emphasis on synthesis, argumentation, and reflection.

* *Week 13: Conclusion – Ethics and the Future of AI**
What does a responsible AI future look like? Recap key themes, revisit philosophical questions, and reflect on individual and collective responsibility in an AI-mediated society.

courses.description:
(UGED2338 is double-coded with FAAS2101.)
Symbols and images that carry traces of Chinese cultural traditions can be found everywhere in the modern world. This course provides a comprehensive overview of the history of Chinese painting and trains students’ abilities in reading images so that they can achieve a deeper understanding of the cultural meanings embedded in everyday encounters. Through a broad survey of Chinese painting from the pre-Song period to the present, students will become familiar with major works, figures, theories, and movements, while also developing fundamental art-historical skills for observing and analyzing images’ style, subject matter, and socio-cultural meaning. In-class discussion of readings and writing exercises will teach students how to read scholarly literature and translate their observations and research on paintings into various forms of writing, such as academic reports, museum labels, or catalogue entries.

courses.course_syllabus:
1. Introduction to the course: Ice breaker

This introductory session will guide students through reading selected entries from Maxwell K. Hearn, *How to Read Chinese* *Paintings* (The Metropolitan Museum of Art and Yale University Press, 2008), to help them understand the basic formats and relationship between imagery and text in Chinese painting.

2. Figural painting (I): Line

This session will introduce major figural paintings from the pre-Song period and examine the historical, cultural, and literary contexts in which they emerged. It also explores the significance of “line” as a fundamental expressive element in Chinese painting.

3. Figural painting (II): Narrative

This session will investigate major figural paintings from the Song period onward and analyze the historical and cultural factors that led to the gradual decline of figural painting as a dominant genre in later periods.

4. Landscape painting (I): Style

This session will analyze the stylistic characteristics of landscape paintings from northern and southern China prior to the Southern Song period and examine the political and philosophical contexts that contributed to the emergence of this new genre as a representative form of Chinese painting.

5. Landscape painting (II): Text and image

This session will explore the relationship between text/poem and image in paintings from the Southern Song period onward, as well as the related yet distinct aesthetic ideals associated with courtly, Buddhist, and literati contexts.

6. Landscape painting (III): Painting schools

This session will examine the specific temporal and spatial conditions, political environment, and social structures that contributed to the emergence of Chinese “painting schools” in the Ming and Qing periods.

7. Paintings genres and art collecting

This session will examine the importance of art collecting within the Chinese political tradition and survey a range of lesser-known genres of Chinese painting, considering their changing significance within major art collections from the Song period to the present.

8. Bird-and-flower painting: Ink and color

This session will examine major bird-and-flower paintings, analyzing their artistic techniques as well as their cultural, political, and literary significance across historical periods.

9. Religious painting (I): Iconography

This session will introduce the transmission, visual features, and theological aspects of Chinese Buddhist and Daoist painting, with particular emphasis on the methods and significance of iconographical research.

10. Religious painting (II): Painting workshop

This session will explore the workshop practices involved in the creation of Chinese paintings, as well as the political and economic contexts in which they emerged.

courses.subject: UGED
courses.title: Chinese Literature in Modern Media
courses.description: This course aims to explore the creative transformation of the Chinese literary tradition in modern media. It seeks to analyze the aesthetic and cultural changes that occur when Chinese literary works are adapted into visual forms. We will compare the similarities and differences between original Chinese literary texts and their comics, animation, film and television adaptations in terms of content, form and artistic techniques. Through a multi-perspective evaluation of works across different media, we will also examine the cultural implications embedded within these adaptations. The course uses classic examples from Chinese literature as a foundation to systematically explore the theories and practices of cross-media adaptations of Chinese literary works. The objective is to cultivate students' ability to appreciate, analyze, and critically evaluate Chinese literature and culture.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for Chinese Studies Majors; and Contemporary China Studies Majors.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
After studying in this course, a student will be able to:

1. Explain the nature, key characteristics, and differences of the two media: text and image.

2. Elucidate major theories and approaches to adapting literary works into film and television, thereby cultivating students’ cross-media capacities for appreciation and critical review.

3. Compare Chinese literary source texts with their multimedia adaptations in terms of content, form, and expressive techniques; analyze the cultural implications involved; and develop multi-perspectival evaluations of works across different media.

courses.description:
(UGED2622 is double-coded with ANTH2530.)

This course examines the pervasiveness of violence from an anthropological and comparative perspective. We consider a wide range of phenomena that can be called violence within diverse historical and cultural contexts. Violence is always political – whether it is manifest in the spectacular practices of torture, terrorism, or genocide, or the invisible structures of inequalities that generate educational, health, and food inequities. Specifically, we will address four SDG goals in depth: SDG#1 No Poverty, SDG #5 “Gender Equality”, SDG# 8 Decent Work and Economic Growth, SDG #10 “Reduced Inequalities” and SDG #16 “Peace, Justice and strong institutions”; The topics covered will be understood in relation to histories of colonialism and nationalism, ideologies about race, gender, and variant forms of social, economic, and political hierarchies. We further examine the effectiveness and limitations of human rights and humanitarianism as remedies, including the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

courses.description: This course aims to inquire into the essence of human existence and its close connection with values consciousness, in order to see that values education is necessary to be "truly human". The contents of the course include reflection on the conditions of human existence in the process of industrialization and globalization and investigation of various conceptions of human existence, such as in Materialism, Evolutionism, Freud, Christianity, Existentialism, Kant and Confucianism. The course concludes that the essence of human existence resides in human subjectivity and values consciousness. Based on such contentions, it will examine the meaning and types of values, and pinpoint the importance of values education to elevate the consciousness of students. Finally it inquires into the meaning of values education and the essence of Aesthetic Education, Religious Education and especially Moral Education in order to recognise their importance in making people "truly human".

courses.title: Ethics and the Human Experience
courses.description:
(UGED2666 is double-coded with ANTH2360.)

This course introduces students to the study of morality and ethics from a social and cross-cultural perspective. Morality and ethics became a distinct area for anthropological inquiry as recently as the beginning of the 21st century. Why this topic is relatively new in anthropology has something to do with the way in which moral differences have been conflated with cultural differences in the history of the discipline. In other words, anthropologists have long presumed that differences between right and wrong, good and bad, are culturally constructed. In recent years, however, this conflation has been questioned and problematized, with reference to the problem of competing moral goods within a single society and the role of the individual in negotiating moral commitments. Having much to say about cultural differences as well as contingent social processes, anthropologists are now in an even better position to contribute to cross-disciplinary conversations about the nature of morality and ethics. By exploring morality and ethics from a social and cross-cultural perspective, this course will demonstrate that morality and ethics is by no means an abstract subject best studied by philosophers. Students will be encouraged to see ethics as a part of their everyday lives, and to see the lives of others as shaped by shared human problems such as how to get along with other people, and how to get along with oneself.

This course is divided into four major units. It begins with an issue highly relevant to university students: the responsibility individuals carry for their own success and self-fulfillment in capitalist societies. The second unit considers why moral and cultural differences have been conflated, and how different societies have responded to shared human problems in different ways. The third unit explores the relationship between morality and the creation and maintenance of social relationships. Case studies of small communities in different parts of the world will be especially helpful for understanding morality and ethics from a social perspective, as cooperation can be fragile yet so important in small communities. Topics and readings in the last unit offer resources for enriching and expanding our vocabulary of virtues. Students will be invited to conduct research into the mundane things ordinary people do to take care of one another in daily life.

courses.title: Contemplative Practices and Holistic Education
courses.description: Holistic education aims at developing human wholeness of students rather than focusing only on achievement and assessment. Contemplative practices, which originated in Asian and Western ancient traditions, have been studied and applied in education, helping professions, and medicine for promoting self-awareness, well-being, mind-body health in the past few decades. This course provides an overview of the philosophical and spiritual roots, cultural influences, and recent scientific studies of contemplative practices in the context of holistic education (SDG#4 Quality education). After introduction of the diverse heritage of contemplative practices in East and West, followed by examining concepts and theories of contemplative practices in disciplines of philosophies, neurosciences, medicine, psychology, and education, students will reflect critically daily life experiences for developing healthy and sustainable lifestyle in the modern world with various contemplative practices (SDG#3 Good health & well-being; SDG#12 Responsible consumption and Production). Ethical attitudes are articulated through building interpersonal connection for cultivating global awareness on topics of peace and justice (SDG#16 Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions). Apart from lectures, interactive tutorial with experiential practice activities, fieldwork, and reflective journal will be included for comprehensive understanding of the topics.

Part I - Contemplative practices in diverse traditions

Students will explore various contemplative practices from the texts in the Eastern and Western traditions from pre-modern to contemporary era.

1. Introduction: Contemplative education in well-being and holistic approaches

- Brief introduction of holistic education and its relationship with contemplative practices and well-being [SDG-GE#3 Good Health and well-being; #4 Quality education]

1. Eastern traditions: Confucian, Taoist, Buddhist, Yogic, etc.

- Examination of some key concepts and contemplative practices in major Chinese and Indian traditions, including Confucian, Taoist, Buddhist, and Yogic traditions

[SDG-GE#3 Good Health and well-being; #4 Quality education]

1. Western traditions: Rumi, Saint Teresa of Avila, Thomas Merton, Emerson, etc.

- Examination of some key concepts and contemplative practices in major Western traditions, including Sufi and early Catholic contemplative traditions

[SDG-GE#3 Good Health and well-being; #4 Quality education]

Part II – Contemplative pedagogy in the holistic education context

Students will apply various contemplative practices for well-being education and related evidence-based research from disciplines of neuroscience, psychology, and holistic education. The interactive tutorial will provide opportunities for students to experience the practices.

1. Attention, concentration and brain state (i.e. centering, mindful sitting)

- Introduction of evidence-based contemplative practices which can improve attention and concentration; practices of mindful sitting and centering are introduced in classroom setting

[SDG-GE#3 Good Health and well-being; #4 Quality education]

[SDG-GE#3 Good Health and well-being; #4 Quality education]

- Introduction of contemplative reading which requires quiet reflection, mindful attentiveness, and letting go of thoughts; contemplative writing requires self-exploration and expression in a quiet classroom setting

[SDG-GE#3 Good Health and well-being; #4 Quality education]

Students will reflect critically on issues of equity, inclusion, and sustainability in community and global level with the knowledge of contemplation.

courses.description: This course aims to discuss the prominent thoughts directing educational practice and their philosophical origins or foundations. Educational thoughts concerning the topics such as the meaning and aims of education, content and practice of teaching and learning will be introduced and examined in relation to various fields of philosophical investigation concerning knowledge and value, humanity and society, etc. Traditional and modern, Chinese and Western perspectives on education will be scrutinized.

courses.learning_outcomes:
The course aims to discuss the prominent thoughts directing educational practice and their philosophical origins or foundations. Besides, it also aims to enhance students' thinking about education by initiating them into philosophically informed educational thoughts, thereby acquiring the mechanism of 'resourcing' oneself within 'the virtuous circle of the enhancement of thinking and the enrichment of thought' (強化思考與深化思想的良性循環中得以開源成泉). After examining some basic educational concepts and ideals concerning the nature and values of education, the course will focus on aims of education as embedded in the educational practice of cultivating desirable human qualities in educated persons, moving from general themes (in Part 1) to special themes (in Part 2), built-in with a series of workshops on thinking through reading and writing「讀寫進思工作坊」**'RAW** Thinking Workshop' based on 'CAROL' method (employing the ACCESS approach for thinking 「六維四體進思法」developed by Roger Cheng).

Students are expected to:

(1)Be able to thoughtfully think about how to tackle three fundamental questions concerning the nature, values and aims of education: (a) what is education? (b) why is education desirable or valuable? (c) how is education is to be practised (concerning its aims, stages and dimensions)? Answering these questions is expected to draw on educational perspectives to be known as in (2).

(2)Be able to master substantive knowledge concerning four philosophically informed educational perspectives as possible answers to the above three questions: (a) 'fivefold education' for the whole person currently discussed in Hong Kong (五育觀、全人教育觀) ; (b) 'perfectionist education' advocated by Wang Kuowei (王國維之完人教育觀) as representing the modem presentation of the traditional Chinese educational thought; (c) the ideal of education for 'autonomy' advocated by the modem West, especially liberalism (自由教育觀); (d) 'quality-based education' (品育觀)-- education as the cultivation of desirable human qualities (SAVE: attitudes-virtues as qualities of hearts 心性;skills-excellences as qualities of powers 才力) based on the neo-Aristotelian perspective in relation to quality education (素質教育) advocated in the mainland China.

(3)Be interested in and be able to think thoughtfully about at least one of the five special dimensions of the 'whole person education' with a sufficient philosophical depth: (a) intellectual education; (b) moral education; (c) social education; (d) aesthetic education; and (e) spiritual education, in relation to the substantive knowledge on educational perspectives as well as their own educational experiences (at home, in school and/or in the university).

(4)Be ready to tryto pursue their own lines of thinking with the assistance of the 'CAROL' criteria embodied in the course of learning (including lectures and workshops) and assessment (mid term workshop serves for both 50% summative and formative assessments). Thus, they are encouraged to present their thoughts according to the 'CAROL' method of five criteria: **(A)** to articulate how problems of education (general problems concerning nature, values and aims of education based on certain educational perspectives, or special problems about dimensions of education) could be (C) critically discussed in drawing from (L) lectures and (R) required readings and (O) one's own thinking and experience.

courses.title: Exploring Sign Languages and Deaf Communities
courses.description: The course aims to introduce to students conceptions and misconceptions about sign language and deaf community. Crucially it explores how deaf and hearing people perceive sign language and deafness and how such perceptions from the hearing and deaf communities might lead to ideological conflicts in the preservation of socio-cultural values of the deaf community and its language, in the methodology and technology of speech and language rehabilitation, and in the mode of deaf education. The course will address these conflicting ideologies from the perspectives of linguistics, sociology, cultural studies, psychology, medicine and education.

courses.title: Reflections on Everyday Life
courses.description:
This course provides an opportunity for students to reflect on the formation of "self" in society and how the society affects our understanding of love, consumption, education, work, and meaning of life. Selected references in sociology, psychology, religion and literature will be introduced to provide a board intellectual perspective to understand the complex relationships between self and society. Students are expected to acquire an ability to analyze and critique on how different social institutions such as education, religion, family, media, work, consumerism, state, etc., affect our attitude and behaviors in some essential issues of life such as mate choice. Following the tradition of critical theory, this course assumes that this reflection is the first step for liberating from "bad faith" and living an authentic life.

Through reflection on experience that affects them most, students are encouraged to critically examine sustainability issues concerning the well-beings of young people (topic 1, 2, 3 and SDG3), quality of education (topic 4 and SDG4), sustainability in the workplace (topic 5 and SDG8) and inequalities in the local context (topic 3, 4, 5 and SDG10).

courses.course_syllabus:
Fundamental Concepts

Social control, social norms, self, role, socialization, internalization, interpretation, definition of situation, world-taken-for-granted, ideology, bad faith, dependence, conformity, sense of security, freedom, autonomy, spontaneity.

Selected topics

1. Self and Society – discusses the “bad faith” and possibility of freedom in everyday life; and the “presentation of self”. Major concepts introduced: social control, social norms, self, role, socialization, internalization, interpretation, definition of situation, world-taken-for-granted, ideology, bad faith, dependence, conformity, sense of security, freedom, autonomy.

1. Love in a Commercialized World – discusses the rise of romantic love and the deceptive nature of erotic love, the making of the “modern traditional” family illustrated by the case of wedding; and how the commercialized world and the individualization process in post-industrial society further erode the “art of loving”. Major concepts introduced: self, role, dependence, sense of security, individualization, capitalism, modernity, post-modernity.

1. Digital Selves in the Online World – discusses the making and presentation of multiple selves since the digital revolution and consumer society; has the “one dimensional man” turned to be a genuine individual in the internet or becoming more monotonous and “one dimensional”? Major concepts: digital age, consumer society, freedom, autonomy, spontaneity, resistance, selves.

1. The Social Construction of Childhood and Modern Education – discusses the “discovery of childhood” and the emergence of the “priceless child” in the capitalist economy. Major concepts: socialization, parenting, value of education and learning.

1. courses.description:
(UGED3208 is double-coded with GDRS3004.)

This course reviews basic concepts, theories and research findings of romantic love and intimate relationship. Various aspects of romantic love and intimate relationship will be critically reviewed. Based on research from a wide range of disciplines including gender studies, cultural studies, sociology, psychology, counselling, media studies, among various fields, together with input from literature and popular culture, the course will cover major areas such as the following: how do we understand the notions of “love” and “intimacy” in the different social and personal contexts, what are the different stages in a relationship; the influence of cultural myths and social scripts; interpersonal processes within romantic relationships (such as attraction, social cognition, communication and conflicts, etc.); how social gender role shapes romantic feelings and behaviors; notions of equality and freedom within relationships; power and violence; intimate relationship across life span, etc.

Students are encouraged to actively reflect upon their own life experience, to engage in critical discussions of cultural phenomenon through case studies, and learn to untangle the cultural myths, norms, and stereotypes that shapes our private lives and our society in general.

Upon the completion of the course, students should demonstrate basic understanding of structure, functions, dynamics, and development of romantic love and other interpersonal relationship. The personal is political. As personal relationships are the most basic social relationships that makes up the larger network of social relationships, it is hope that students could use knowledge from this course as an insight to understand, develop, and improve the quality of their own interpersonal relationship, and would aspire to build a more open and equal society starting from equalitarian and mindful personal relationships.

Through critical exercise and personal reflection on notions and experience of Love and Intimate Relationship in relations to notions such as power, diversity, equality, and freedom, the course engages directly with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 by engaging directly with the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality), 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institution).

courses.description:
(UGED3322 is double-coded with CURE3145.)

This course studies Buddhism and contemporary life in the context of the new development of Buddhism. It examines how Buddhism is reinvented and reconceptualized to make it meaningful for men and women living in modern complex society of the information age. Based on the recent development of Buddhism in both Asia and in the West, this course discusses how Buddhism responds to contemporary issues facing contemporary men and women. Topics include the Buddhist approach to economic development and human right, pollution and biotechnology, feminism, Buddhist ethics and the issues of abortion, euthanasia and suicide, Buddhism and interfaith dialogue.
